Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

I kept the marker visible above the mulch and recorded the row numbers the measured pressure the length of replacement pipe and the two bag labels in the repair log the orchard manager asked whether we could run the whole lower block for its usual cycle but I said we had only tested the repaired section and had not yet checked every emitter from row twelve to row eighteen period he said to keep the usual cycle off until the filter check was done and to leave the blue handwheel where Rosa had set it period when we left, water was no longer crossing the lane, the lower block remained above the stated threshold, and the afternoon filter check was still pending period", "output": "We reached the east orchard at six fifteen on Tuesday after the night crew reported water running across the access lane. The repair was at the lower irrigation manifold beside rows twelve through eighteen, not at the pump house as the first radio message said. That distinction mattered because the pump house was already scheduled for a separate filter check.

I met Rosa by the steel gate, and she showed me the wet ground and the drop in pressure on the gauge. The upper block still had a steady reading, but the lower block was down to eleven pounds per square inch. She said, “The trees are not dry yet, but the far end is barely dripping.” “Right,” I said. “That is the south supply, and we should check the valve before we blame the emitters.” Rosa had isolated that block at the blue handwheel, but she had not closed the main feed because the packing nut was weeping a little and she did not want to force it.

We walked the line from the manifold toward row eighteen and marked three places where the soil was soft. The first was near a splice under the grass, the second was beside a buried sleeve, and the third was close to a root crossing. We did not dig at all three spots at once because the irrigation map was old and the marked trench did not line up with the current row stakes. Instead, we used the acoustic probe and checked the surface for a pressure change after Rosa opened the lower block for a moment. At the first mark, we heard a faint hiss, but it faded when the line settled. At the sleeve, the probe stayed quiet. At the root crossing, the ground pulsed with each turn of the pressure regulator.

Before we opened anything, I asked for the last repair notes and found a note from Eli saying the sleeve had been replaced in April with a wider coupling. Marta read the note aloud and then said in German, “Er kommt um sechs,” and added that he would arrive at six to bring the spare clamp. Eli had not arrived yet, so we used the clamp from the truck stock and left his box untouched. Marta also told the crew in Portuguese, “Pois é,” meaning “Yeah, that is right,” when Rosa confirmed the lower block was the only area showing the pressure loss. No one treated either phrase as a filler; they answered the information and kept working.

We uncovered the root crossing by hand and found a split in the poly line about eight inches past the regulator. The break was on the downstream side of the old sleeve, not on the sleeve itself. There was a shallow scrape on the upper surface and a longer crack along the underside. We shut the lower block and waited until the gauge reached zero before cutting the damaged section. Rosa said, “Leave enough line to make two clean cuts,” so we measured from the crack instead of cutting right beside it. The first cut showed a thin wall where the pipe had rubbed against a stone, and the second cut was round and firm. We removed the stone and put it in the debris bucket so it would not roll back into the trench.

For the numbered repair check, I dictated five points:
1. The replacement pipe was the same outside diameter and pressure rating as the existing line.
2. Both cut ends were square and free of grit before the barbed coupling went in.
3. The clamps sat behind the raised ridges and were tightened evenly with the hand driver.
4. We left the coupling uncovered while we tested it.
5. The removed piece and the stone went into separate bags for the maintenance log.

I checked each point as Rosa called it back, and she checked the written labels against the bags before we moved on.

We reopened the lower block slowly and watched the gauge while water filled the repaired section. The pressure climbed to twenty-seven pounds and held there for four minutes. We saw no fresh water at the coupling, and the three marked spots stayed dry, but the row eighteen emitters were still weaker than the ones nearer the manifold. That did not mean the repair had fixed every problem. The screen filter could still be partly blocked, and the regulator might need a separate adjustment. We agreed to leave those checks for the afternoon unless the pressure dropped again before then.

There was one condition in the field plan that we had to keep in view: if the gauge fell below twenty pounds during the next half hour, we were to close the lower block and call Luis before disturbing the filter housing. If it stayed above twenty pounds, we could finish backfilling around the line and put the temporary marker at the repair point. Rosa repeated the condition to me and wrote the time beside the gauge reading. At ten thirty, the gauge showed twenty-six pounds and the ground around the coupling was dry, so we began to replace the soil in layers without packing it hard against the pipe.

I kept the marker visible above the mulch and recorded the row numbers, the measured pressure, the length of replacement pipe, and the two bag labels in the repair log. The orchard manager asked whether we could run the whole lower block for its usual cycle, but I said we had only tested the repaired section and had not yet checked every emitter from row twelve to row eighteen. He said to keep the usual cycle off until the filter check was done and to leave the blue handwheel where Rosa had set it. When we left, water was no longer crossing the lane, the lower block remained above the stated threshold, and the afternoon filter check was still pending."}]
